params.question: What was India's approximate Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) per 100,000 live births around 2001, prior to the launch of NHM?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 75 per 100,000 is the WHO-recommended threshold for high-performing health systems. India's pre-NHM MMR was four times higher — approximately 300 per 100,000 live births.
India's pre-NHM MMR was approximately 300 per 100,000 live births — double this figure, and four times the WHO threshold of 75.

Correct. India's MMR around 2001 was approximately 300 per 100,000 live births — four times the WHO threshold of less than 75. This stark burden, concentrated in high-focus states, was a key driver for creating the National Health Mission.
500 per 100,000 would place India among the highest globally. The pre-NHM MMR was approximately 300 — still alarmingly high at four times the WHO threshold, but not this extreme.

overallFeedback.feedback: India's MMR around 2001 was approximately 300 per 100,000 live births — four times higher than the WHO threshold of 75. This figure, alongside an IMR of 66 per 1,000 live births, was the core epidemiological burden that NHM was designed to address.

Well done! India's pre-NHM MMR of approximately 300 per 100,000 live births — alongside an IMR of 66 per 1,000 and high neonatal mortality — was the epidemiological imperative that drove creation of the National Health Mission.

params.question: Why was a programme like RBSK necessary even after RMNCH+A established the mother-child continuum of care?

answers.text: Because RMNCH+A lacked a financial protection component for sick neonates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Financial protection for mothers and sick neonates is the mandate of JSSK (Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram), not RBSK. RBSK addresses a different limitation of the passive health system.

answers.text: Because conditions like congenital heart disease and developmental delays remain undetected without active screening of children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. RMNCH+A's ANC/delivery/HBNC pathway serves mothers and newborns but does not actively screen growing children. RBSK fills this gap by deploying Mobile Health Teams to screen all children 0–18 years for the 4Ds — Birth Defects, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental Delays — with referral to District Early Intervention Centres.

answers.text: Because adolescents were invisible in India's earlier MCH architecture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adolescent invisibility is the specific gap that RKSK (Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram) addresses. RBSK targets a different problem — the silent burden of undetected birth defects, diseases, deficiencies, and developmental delays in children.

answers.text: Because immunisation coverage had stagnated despite the Universal Immunisation Programme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The immunisation coverage plateau was addressed by Mission Indradhanush, not RBSK. RBSK specifically targets early identification of the 4Ds in children through systematic screening.

overallFeedback.feedback: RBSK was created because the RMNCH+A continuum, while effective for maternal and newborn care, does not actively screen children beyond the neonatal period. Conditions like congenital heart disease or developmental delay would go undetected in a passive system — RBSK's Mobile Health Teams screen all children 0–18 years for the 4Ds.

Exactly. A passive, symptom-driven health system misses silent conditions in children. RBSK's active screening for the 4Ds — via Mobile Health Teams screening all children 0–18 years — fills a gap that the RMNCH+A continuum alone could not address.

interactions.label: Institutional delivery in India increased from approximately 40% (NFHS-3) to 79%

params.question: Institutional delivery in India increased from approximately 40% (NFHS-3) to 79% (NFHS-5). Which pair of NHM interventions is most directly responsible for this shift?

answers.text: RBSK mobile screening teams and RKSK adolescent health services

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: RBSK screens children for the 4Ds and RKSK provides adolescent health services. Neither addresses the financial or geographic barriers that previously kept women from delivering in health facilities.

answers.text: Mission Indradhanush catch-up campaigns and ICDS nutrition programmes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mission Indradhanush targets immunisation coverage and ICDS addresses child malnutrition. While critical NHM programmes, neither directly incentivises or enables institutional delivery.

answers.text: JSY conditional cash transfers and JSSK free-services guarantees

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana) provides conditional cash transfers to incentivise facility-based delivery, while JSSK guarantees free delivery care, diagnostics, medicines, blood, and transport — together removing the financial and geographic barriers that previously kept women delivering at home.

answers.text: RMNCH+A strategic framework and HBNC postnatal home visits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: RMNCH+A provides the overarching care continuum and HBNC covers postnatal home visits by ASHAs. While important, the specific interventions that directly drove the institutional delivery increase were JSY (cash incentive to deliver in a facility) and JSSK (free facility services).

overallFeedback.feedback: The institutional delivery increase is directly attributable to two complementary NHM interventions: JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana), which provides conditional cash transfers to incentivise facility delivery, and JSSK, which guarantees free delivery care, transport, and diagnostics — together removing the barriers that kept women delivering at home.

Well analysed. The institutional delivery revolution is directly attributable to JSY's demand-side cash incentive and JSSK's supply-side free-services guarantee — together removing both financial and geographic barriers to facility-based delivery.
